fields.meta_title: Employment Verification Letter Sample and Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What an employment verification letter confirms, a short sample, and an app that drafts each letter from your HR records. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build an Employment Verification Letter Generator for HR
fields.hero_description: An employment verification letter confirms someone's job and dates of service. Describe how HR handles requests, and Emergent builds the request form and the letter behind it.
fields.features_heading: What Goes Into a Verification Letter
fields.features_subheading: An employment verification letter template covers the wording. Emergent adds the request form and the HR sign-off.
fields.feature_1:
One request form for every requester

Asks who wants the letter and why, then changes the questions to suit them. A landlord gets a short set, while a lender gets the longer one its own underwriter needs.
fields.feature_2:
Letters drafted from the HR record

Pulls the job title and start date straight from your employee table into the letter. Nobody retypes a hire date from memory or edits the copy someone saved two years ago.
fields.feature_3:
Salary only when the employee agrees

Adds base pay to a letter only when the employee has said yes on the request form. Every other letter confirms the job and its dates and leaves compensation out entirely.
fields.feature_4:
A signature before anything is sent

Sends each draft to the HR manager to read and sign on screen. Nothing leaves the app unsigned, and a draft left sitting for a full day sends the manager a reminder.
fields.feature_5:
A record of every letter you sent

Logs each request beside the letter it produced, with the signer and send date, in a database you own. When a lender calls back next spring, the exact letter is one search away.
fields.feature_6:
Room for the next request type

Next quarter it might be letters in Spanish, or a nightly sync with your payroll system. Prompt the change, or let an HR engineer pick it up in the exported GitHub repo.

fields.tab_content_1:
Lender forms answered from the payroll record

A lender's Form 1005 arrives as a PDF with the borrower's signed authorization. Emergent reads the fields it asks for and fills hire date, title and base pay from your HR table. A payroll approver signs off on each reply before it goes back, and the log records which lender received it.
fields.tab_content_2:
A signed letter for the landlord, salary optional

Employees request a letter from a short form that asks who it is addressed to and whether salary should appear. The HR manager signs, and the landlord receives a PDF on company letterhead stating the job title and full-time status.
fields.tab_content_3:
Dates and the final title, with one Missouri exception

Anyone with an end date gets a narrower letter: first day, last day and final title, reviewed by an HR generalist. In Missouri, leavers with 90 days of service at a corporation of seven or more can write by certified mail within a year. They get a service letter within 45 days stating why they left.
fields.tab_content_4:
No signed release, no answer

Screening firms use a verification page instead of calling HR. The firm names the candidate and uploads the signed release, and the app checks dates and title against the employee table. A request without a release goes back to the firm with a note, and the app confirms dates once the release is on file.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Verification Letter
fields.howto_description: The hard part comes before the first request: deciding which facts HR will confirm, and for whom. Steps 1 and 2 settle that, and the other five turn the answer into a signed letter.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Check who is asking and why
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Put it on letterhead with a signer
fields.howto_step_1_des: Confirm the request names the employee and says what the letter is for, such as a lease or a mortgage. Ask for the employee's written consent before you confirm anything, even a start date, and keep that consent with the request.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Most letters confirm full name, job title, start date and whether the person works full or part time. If someone changed roles, give the current title and the date they took it. Reasons for leaving stay out unless a state law requires them.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Print the verification of employment letter on company letterhead and address it to the requester by name. Close with an HR signature above a printed name, plus a direct phone number a landlord or lender can call to check it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: If the request and the HR system disagree on a title or start date, ask the employee which one is wrong. A promotion payroll never recorded, or a rehire with two start dates, is the usual cause. Correct the record, then draft.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Add a review step for exceptions
fields.howto_step_5_des: Route odd requests to a second reader before they go out, such as one asking you to state weekly hours or a letter addressed to a court. Routine letters for current staff can go straight to the signer for a quick read and signature.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Send it to the requester directly
fields.howto_step_6_des: Email the signed PDF to the address on the request, or upload it to the lender's portal. A letter that reaches the landlord from your HR inbox is harder to question than one the employee forwards from a personal account.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Set how long letters are kept
fields.howto_step_7_des: Agree on a retention period with counsel and apply it as you would to personnel files. If a former employee later says a letter got their dates wrong, the signed copy is what settles it.

findings.fix: Keep the template-vs-app contrast in one intro only. Give the other a different job, e.g. the how-to intro names the decision HR has to make before the first letter goes out.

findings.quote: feature_5 "Logs each request beside the letter it produced, with the signer and send date" / howto_step_7_des "Store every signed letter next to the request it answered."; tab_content_3 "An HR generalist reviews each one before release." / howto_step_5_des "Send unusual letters to a second person before they go out, such as anything for a former employee"
findings.issue: Two ideas are each said twice with the words swapped. The letter is filed beside its request in feature 5 and step 7, and former-employee letters get a second reviewer in tab 3 and step 5. The previous fix moved step 7's reason but kept its first sentence.
findings.fix: Step 7 opens on what is new (the retention period, the dispute that the signed copy settles). Step 5 uses a different exception (a request for weekly hours, a letter addressed to a court), because tab 3 already covers former employees.

findings.quote: feature_4 "Nothing leaves the app unsigned"; tab_content_1 "Nothing goes back to the lender until someone in payroll approves the reply"; tab_content_4 "nothing is confirmed until the release is on file"
findings.issue: The same "Nothing X until Y" gate sentence appears three times across features and tabs. Tab 3's H3 "nothing more" and tab 4's H3 "No signed release, no answer" make the negation pattern more obvious still, and the repeated cadence reads as machine-written.
findings.fix: Keep at most one. Say the others positively and specifically, e.g. tab 1 "Ana in payroll approves each reply, and only then does it go back to the lender"; tab 4 "The app confirms dates once the release is uploaded".

findings.quote: "In Missouri, a former employee who asks in writing by certified mail can get a service letter within 45 days that also states why they left."
findings.issue: Stated for every former employee, but Mo. Rev. Stat. 290.140 applies only to corporations with 7+ employees and to people with at least 90 days of service who request within one year of leaving, citing the statute. As written, the sentence is untrue for many Missouri employers and leavers. The prior cycle logged this as a note; it is a legal statement of fact that is wrong as worded, so it blocks.
findings.fix: Qualify it: "In Missouri, an eligible former employee (90+ days of service, employer with 7 or more staff) who asks by certified mail within a year can get a service letter within 45 days that states why they left." Or say "Missouri's service letter law can require..." and keep the conditions in the source record.

findings.quote: H3 "Dates of service and the final title, nothing more"
findings.issue: The H3 promises nothing more, then the paragraph adds a reason for leaving for Missouri requests.
findings.fix: Frame Missouri as the exception in the H3, or drop "nothing more" (this also helps the #22 finding).

findings.quote: "Next quarter it might be letters in Spanish, or a nightly sync with your payroll system."
findings.issue: Five feature bodies open on a product verb and this one opens on a hedged hypothetical. It is a full sentence, so it does not block.
findings.fix: Open on what happens, e.g. "Adds Spanish letters or a nightly payroll sync when you prompt for them..."
